newsitem.title: UK: Market struggles to value demerged Brit Gas.
newsitem.headline: Market struggles to value demerged Brit Gas.

text.p: While British Gas shareholders are set to give the green light to the utility's planned break-up next Wednesday, industry analysts are struggling to value the trading arm which will be hived off from the transport business.
The new firm, to be called Centrica, has already said it won't pay dividends in the short-term, so analysts are looking at the firm's assets to establish Centrica's worth.

But how do you value a company which is witnessing whirlwind changes to its business environment? And what are all the asset calculations worth given the takeover rumours flying around since the demerger was announced a year ago?
Given all the uncertainties surrounding Centrica's future, it is no surprise to see wide variations in analysts' valuations on the share, which starts when-issued, or grey market, trading on Monday.
"There are a large number of grey areas and lots of assumptions to make," said analyst Irene Himona at broker SocGen, echoing a widely held view.
Himona sees a trading range for Centrica shares of between 61 and 82 pence. But in a recent report Merrill Lynch analyst Andrew Wright tags a price to Centrica of 40 pence per share.

About the only certainty about Centrica is that it will face many challenges as its monopoly in gas supply is further dismantled. But Centrica might still be an attractive takeover target for any company that wants to step into the British gas and electricity markets while they are being opened up to competition.

Centrica will house the British Gas supply and trading business in Britain along with its Morecombe Bay gas fields. The rest of British Gas -- its international gas, oil and gas exploration businesses and gas pipeline and storage company Transco -- will trade as BG Plc.

The takeover rumour mill worked overtime last year, spinning out the names of British Petroleum Co Plc and Shell as possible buyers of Centrica. BP declined to comment, while Shell denied it was interested.

British Gas has already been hard hit by rival oil companies in the gas market for big industrial users. Here the utility has seen its market share slump to below 35 percent since competition was introduced in the early 1990s.
Now it is Centrica's task to limit damage in the domestic market, which will be opened up to full competition nationwide in 1998.

In addition, the company is saddled with the "take-or-pay" contracts, which British Gas has been trying to renegotiate. The contracts oblige it to buy fixed amounts of gas at set prices from North Sea gas producers. Many of the deals were signed before privatisation in 1986.
But as British Gas saw its share in the market for big industrial users dwindle, it had to pay for more gas than it could sell.
The contracts were one of the main reasons for British Gas's demerger as it wants to protect the money-spinning Transco pipeline transport operations from the take-or-pay burden.
So far British Gas has successfully renegotiated take-or-pay contracts with one of its own units, BP and Mobil Corp.

Details of these deals have given analysts some clues about the costs of striking new contracts, but it is unclear what the total costs will be as Centrica is currently assessing how many more deals it wants to conclude.

Such uncertainties also surround BG Plc, the re-named British Gas rump. BG faces tough proposals from industry regulator Ofgas which wants to curb the fees BG can charge gas suppliers for transporting their gas through its pipelines.
The proposals, which are currently being vetted by the Monopolies and Merger Commission (MMC), would results in a sharp dividend cut.
But nobody knows wether they will be left intact by the MMC, which is expected to report by April at the earliest.
With analysts differing on how to asses BG -- on its asset base or via the dividend yield method -- valuations for the company vary somewhere between 160 and 220 pence per share.
But analysts generally agree that of the two, Centrica offers the best investment, referring to the regulatory framework that will constrain BG.
In contrast, Centrica will probably appeal because of a potential takeover premium, analysts said.
"Any company with 19 million customers must be generating at least some takeover interest," said Nigel Hawkins at Yamaichi.
Grey market trading in both Centrica and BG will start on Monday, offering an early indication of investor interest before the demerger has offically taken place.
